ddx.step1_summary: - Chief complaint: progressive left arm numbness/tingling with functional weakness and intermittent numbness extending from elbow to hand; accompanying neck pain; transient left-eye visual disturbance reported previously. - Symptom details: onset of left-arm numbness about two weeks ago during boxing class, gradually worsening; numbness involves elbow, arm, and some fingers; tingling in fingertips; occasional weakness affecting grip (difficulty holding objects, piano); pain not primary; resting or massage/hot baths did not help. Visual symptom: transient partial loss of peripheral vision in the left eye for about 20 minutes. Fatigue and occasional headaches noted. - Aggravating/relieving factors: boxing activity possibly contributing; rest does not improve numbness; no relief with massage or warm baths. - Past medical history: recent heavy cold/flu about a month ago; no major chronic medical problems reported; uses ibuprofen for muscle soreness; takes vitamin D; iron supplements sporadically (GP advised); sometimes Melatonin. - Medications/allergies: ibuprofen, vitamin D, iron supplements (infrequently), Melatonin; no reported drug allergies. - Family/social history: father with hypothyroidism and autoimmune issues; mother with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia; no stated neurological family history. Social: active with boxing; alcohol use around a month ago (uncharacteristic heavy drinking). - Vital signs/exam findings: not provided in transcript. - Labs/imaging: doctor plans an urgent neurology referral and brain imaging (MRI) as part of work-up; no labs/imaging results yet mentioned. - Red flags noted by clinician: transient vision change, unilateral limb symptoms with weakness, neck pain, and activity-related onset prompting concern for central nervous system/ demyelinating or vascular etiologies; discussion of MS as a possibility and need for MRI.

V: Ischemic cerebrovascular event (e.g., transient ischemic attack with amaurosis fugax) – rationale: unilateral left-arm numbness/weakness and transient left-eye vision disturbance raise concern for vascular source with cerebral or retinal ischemia; boxing-related neck strain could contribute; however, event duration and progression over weeks are atypical for a classic TIA
I: Autoimmune/inflammatory demyelinating disease (e.g., MS presenting with optic neuritis and spinal/neuraxial sensory symptoms) – rationale: episode of transient left-eye vision change plus unilateral arm numbness/weakness and family autoimmune history; MS can present with optic symptoms and sensory deficits in different sites over time
N: Neoplasm (e.g., brain/spinal cord lesion) – rationale: new focal neurological symptoms; though less likely given subacute, fluctuating course rather than a progressive mass effect, it remains possible without imaging
D: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy / cervical radiculopathy – rationale: neck pain with left-arm numbness and weakness; could reflect nerve root or spinal cord involvement related to degenerative changes; boxing could precipitate or worsen
I2: Iatrogenic/intoxication – rationale: recent heavy alcohol use and NSAID use could contribute to non-specific symptoms, but unlikely to explain focal unilateral arm numbness and transient monocular vision loss
C: Congenital neuropathies or anatomical variations – rationale: less likely given acute/subacute presentation, but could contribute to nerve distribution symptoms if present
A: Autoimmune/Allergic processes other than MS (e.g., other inflammatory neuropathies) – rationale: autoimmune milieu in family could predispose to CNS/PN inflammatory processes
T: Traumatic injury to neck/shoulder or brachial plexus from boxing – rationale: boxing activity is ongoing and could cause local trauma contributing to arm numbness; however would not fully explain transient vision loss
E: Endocrine/Metabolic neuropathies (e.g., B12 deficiency, diabetes, hypothyroidism) – rationale: family history of endocrine/aut autoimmune disease; could contribute to neuropathic symptoms, though focal presentation is less typical

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis (MS) with demyelinating manifestations (optic neuritis with limb sensory symptoms)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Young-to-middle-aged adult with transient monocular vision disturbance and unilateral limb numbness/weakness in a time-separated manner fits MS relapse–remission pattern. Family history of autoimmune disease supports autoimmune etiology. Neck pain and boxing-related activity do not exclude MS. The clinician highlighted MS as a consideration and scheduled urgent neurology evaluation with neuroimaging.
supporting_evidence: Left arm numbness/weakness with sensory distribution (2nd–4th digits, palm side) and grip difficulty
Episodes over weeks with progression rather than a single acute event
Family history of autoimmune disease in father
Age group typical for demyelinating diseases
opposing_evidence: Optic symptoms duration shorter than typical optic neuritis which often persists days to weeks
No prior MS diagnosis or clear multiple neurologic episodes documented yet

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack / amaurosis fugax (vascular etiology)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute unilateral symptoms (left-arm numbness) plus transient monocular vision loss raise vascular etiologies such as TIA with amaurosis fugax. Boxing-related neck strain could contribute to vascular compromise. However, the subacute progression over two weeks and lack of vascular risk factors make this less classic.
supporting_evidence: Age 40s–50s (vascular etiologies possible though less common without risk factors)
opposing_evidence: TIAs are typically sudden, focal events rather than gradual, progressing symptoms over two weeks
No established vascular risk factors described (diabetes, hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia) in transcript

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Cervical radiculopathy or cervical spondylotic myelopathy
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Neck pain with unilateral arm numbness/weakness and sensory changes can reflect nerve root or spinal cord compression from cervical degenerative disease, potentially exacerbated by boxing-related neck strain.
supporting_evidence: Weakness and difficulty with tasks requiring fine motor control (piano) in left hand
Distribution could align with cervical nerve roots (potential C6–C8 involvement)
opposing_evidence: Transient visual disturbance is not explained by cervical pathology
Symptoms describe both elbow-to-hand involvement and specific finger numbness that could be more diffuse than classic radiculopathy

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Median nerve–related neuropathy / carpal tunnel or focal peripheral neuropathy
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Numbness in 2nd–4th fingers on the palm side with grip difficulty could reflect median nerve involvement; boxing and repetitive hand use could contribute. However, involvement from elbow to hand and concurrent neck pain makes a pure focal median neuropathy less likely as the sole diagnosis.
supporting_evidence: Numbness in 2nd–4th fingers on the palmar side
Weak grip and difficulty with fine motor tasks (piano)
opposing_evidence: Symptoms extend to the elbow and include neck pain; carpal tunnel typically presents with nocturnal symptoms and predominantly hand-based complaints
